channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Italian industrial output rose 1.2% in September from August after an unexpected 1.2% fall in August, and the third-quarter average was down 0.4%, ISTAT data show, MarketScreener reports.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports, citing the national statistics bureau ISTAT, that industrial output in Italy increased by 1.2% month on month in September after an unexpected 1.2% drop in August. Average output in the third quarter was down 0.4%, after a 0.3% increase in the previous three months. On a work day-adjusted year-on-year basis, output fell 0.1% in September after a 0.2% rise in August, which was revised from an originally reported flat reading. The row does not give the breakdown by sector, the level of output or any forecast for the fourth quarter.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports an aggregate output index, not figures for chemicals, construction materials or vehicles. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a monthly rebound that leaves the quarter lower indicates flat to weak manufacturing demand for inputs, and a revised August shows the data are volatile. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Italy is a large European manufacturing and construction market, so weak industrial output points to soft demand for industrial bonding, sealing and coating materials there; the row gives no sector or volume figures. Points that may be worth considering include Italian output for October and the sector split of the September figure.

MarketScreener

item.title: Germany's population fell 0.1% in 2025 to about 83.5 million and by a further 0.2% in the first half of 2026, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports, saying forecasts of demand for new housing construction need re-evaluating.
item.description:
Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that the Federal Institute for Research on Building, Urban Affairs and Spatial Development (BBSR) and other current forecasts still assume a high demand for new housing construction, but that the new demographic development requires a re-evaluation of that demand. The population rose continuously between 2011 and 2024, except in 2020, and began to decline in 2025: about 83.5 million people lived in Germany at the end of 2025, 0.1% or around 110,000 fewer than a year earlier, and in the first half of 2026 the population fell by 0.2%, around 168,000 more. The paper attributes the decline to both the natural population trend and international migration: the persistent birth deficit, with more deaths than births, could no longer be offset by net immigration in 2025, annual immigration from abroad has kept falling, including in the first half of 2026, and a further decline is to be expected if net immigration stays low and the birth deficit continues. The row does not name the statistical source of the figures, give the BBSR's housing demand estimate, regional differences, household numbers or any effect on construction activity.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports population figures and a newspaper's view that housing demand forecasts need revising, not construction or permit data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, housing demand depends on the number and size of households as well as on population, so a small population decline does not by itself reduce demand for new building, but it weakens one of the drivers on which demand forecasts rest, and regional differences are likely. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and renovation are large end-markets, and a lower outlook for new housing could shift weight toward renovation and refurbishment, which also use bonding, sealing and coating materials; the row gives no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include German building permits and completions, the BBSR's next housing demand estimate and net immigration data.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: A McKinsey Global Institute study of 6,000 traded products, covering USD 19 trillion of imports, finds 23% face two of three supply vulnerabilities, against 15% in 2000, and 4% face all three.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) examined the potential for supply disruption of 6,000 products that account for USD 19 trillion of imports worldwide, based on whether they were critical to broader economic activity, were concentrated in one or a small number of locations, or were sourced from a potentially hostile country. It found that nearly one in four traded goods is vulnerable to supply disruptions that could have damaging consequences for the importing economies, that 23% of the products face two sources of vulnerability, up from 15% in 2000, and that only 4% face all three, including US imports of rare-earth magnets and smartphones from China. The row does not give the year of the 23% figure or say whether the 15% in 2000 covers the same products, which chemical or materials products are among them, how a country is judged "potentially hostile", how the 4% and 23% shares are weighted by value or how they differ by importing region.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a study's exposure measure, not a disruption that has occurred. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, products that are concentrated in a few locations or sourced from a country seen as potentially hostile are the ones where export controls, tariffs or conflicts can interrupt supply, and a rising share points to growing exposure of importers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, specialty raw materials, additives and intermediates are sometimes sourced from a few producers or countries, so the study's three criteria are one lens through which importers' supply bases can be assessed; the row names no chemical products. Points that may be worth considering include any chemical products named in the full study.

MarketScreener

item.title: Spain held its first full-day general strike in 14 years on 11 November over housing costs, hitting car plants and ports, with union figures of 40% to 80% participation in the first hours and employers calling it low, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that the first full-day general strike in Spain in 14 years took place two and a half weeks before the parliamentary elections that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez scheduled for 29 November. It was called by the two large union confederations CCOO and UGT and mainly affected large car manufacturers such as VW in Pamplona, wholesale markets and commercial ports such as Algeciras. Union figures show that between 40% and 80% of workers took part in the first hours, depending on the sector, while the employers' association CEOE spoke of low participation. The BBC reports that the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations, which Handelsblatt names as the CEOE, called participation "low and uneven", while UGT head Pepe Álvarez called the strike a success with "massive" participation and CCOO's Unai Sordo called turnout "very significant". The Independent reports that around four million workers took part, with 90% participation in the automotive and port sectors and electricity demand down by up to 15.5%, without naming the source of those figures or giving a baseline for the electricity figure. Business Day reports that the average rental price of EUR 1,176 equals about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain, and that Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which the central bank expects to grow to more than one million by 2028. MarketScreener reports that strikers blocked Madrid's Gran Vía and shops closed. The rows do not give lost output, the duration of any disruption beyond the day, the government's response or any effect on construction sites.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a one-day labour action with conflicting participation figures, not a lasting stoppage. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a general strike interrupts production, logistics and port handling on the day it is held and signals pressure on housing policy before an election. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Spain hosts vehicle assembly, ports and construction activity, so a stoppage delays supplier deliveries and customer output for that day, and housing-affordability policy bears on construction demand; the rows give no output or order figures. Points that may be worth considering include whether further strikes are called, the housing measures that parties propose before the 29 November election and Spanish construction activity data.

Handelsblatt | BBC News | The Independent | Business Day | MarketScreener

item.title: The Washington Institute for Near East Policy counts 37 ships attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October, the most since the US-Iran war began, with 10 more by 10 November, Hong Kong Economic Times reports.
item.description:
Hong Kong Economic Times reports, citing data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, that 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October, the highest number since the US-Iran war began, and that attacks in November show no sign of decreasing, with 10 ships attacked as of 10 November. It adds that the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has confirmed up to 130 incidents in Hormuz since the war began, mostly attacks, in which at least 25 sailors died. The Economic Times, citing Kpler, says traffic through the strait has averaged 10.5 million barrels a day since the start of October, below the pre-war 13.5 million but up substantially from the depths of the disruption. The Straits Times reports that President Trump has said further strikes on Iran would not be necessary but that regional flare-ups have persisted and peace talks have shown little progress. The rows do not give the type, flag or damage of the ships attacked, who carried out the attacks (the rows cited here are silent on this), changes in freight or insurance costs or how traffic responded to the attacks.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report counts of attacks and a traffic estimate, not freight rates, insurance costs or delivery delays. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, attacks on shipping raise war-risk insurance and freight costs and can delay deliveries of oil, petrochemical feedstocks and other cargo even when volumes recover. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher freight and insurance costs and uncertain delivery times reach raw-material and finished-goods logistics; the rows give no cost figures. Points that may be worth considering include the November attack count, Hormuz transit volumes and any US-Iran agreement.

Hong Kong Economic Times | The Economic Times | The Straits Times

item.title: The RICS surveyors' measure of sales expectations for the year ahead fell to minus 17 in October from 1 in September, the weakest since July 2023, and its price expectations index also fell to minus 17, the Financial Times reports.
item.description:
The Financial Times reports, under a headline on pessimism in the UK housing market, that the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors' (RICS) measure of sales expectations for the year ahead fell from 1 in September to minus 17 in October, the weakest reading since July 2023. The RICS index tracking price expectations over the next 12 months fell to minus 17 from zero in September, the lowest since October 2023. The row explains that the indices measure the difference between the proportion of surveyors reporting increases and the proportion reporting decreases in housing market activity, with negative readings meaning that more respondents report falls than rises. The row does not give sales or price levels, the regional split, the number of surveyors, the reasons for the change or any completed-transaction data.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports surveyors' expectations, not completed sales, prices or building activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, weak sales and price expectations tend to precede lower transaction volumes and can reduce owners' willingness to renovate and developers' willingness to start projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, housing is a market for construction and renovation materials, and lower housing activity in the UK, where the row's headline places the survey, would reduce demand for bonding, sealing and coating products; the row gives no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include the next RICS survey, housing activity and mortgage data and central bank decisions.

The Financial Times

item.title: Japan's wholesale prices rose 7.1% in the year to October, above the 6.5% median market forecast, and yen-based import prices rose 24.8%, MarketScreener reports.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Japan's corporate goods price index, a measure of wholesale prices, rose 7.1% year on year in October, faster than the median market forecast of 6.5% and after a 6.8% rise in September. The yen-based import price index rose 24.8% from a year earlier, which the row calls a sign that the weakness of the currency continued to push up the cost of raw material imports. The row says the data will be among the factors the Bank of Japan examines at its next policy meeting on 17 and 18 December. The row does not give the breakdown by product group, the change in dollar-based import prices, the exchange-rate level or the weight of chemicals in the index.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports producer-level prices and yen-based import prices, which mix price changes with exchange-rate effects. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a weak yen raises the yen cost of imported oil and chemical raw materials for Japanese producers, which can feed into selling prices and into the central bank's stance. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japan is a manufacturing market supplied with both local and imported materials, so input-price pressure there may affect customers' costs and pricing discussions; the row gives no figures for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the November price index, the level of the yen and the Bank of Japan's December decision.

MarketScreener

item.title: Mexico's light vehicle production fell 17.7% year on year in October and exports fell 17.9%, INEGI data show, with General Motors' output down 45.5%, El Financiero writes.
item.description:
El Financiero writes, citing INEGI, that light vehicle production in Mexico fell 17.7% year on year in October and that exports fell 17.9%. In the first ten months Nissan cut production by 139,318 units, more than the net decline of the whole industry, so the other automakers together offset only a small part of that loss; the row says this coincides with Nissan's global restructuring and the closure of its CIVAC plant in Morelos and of COMPAS, the plant it shared with Mercedes-Benz in Aguascalientes. General Motors and Stellantis stand out in the October fall: GM's production fell 45.5%, and the row also lists a four-week shutdown at Silao between September and October to adapt to the new generation of Silverado and Sierra pickups, and the end of gasoline Blazer production at Ramos Arizpe, which is being transferred to Tennessee; Jeep Compass production at Toluca fell by nearly 90%. The row does not give production volumes for October or the ten-month industry total, the comparison base for the export fall and for the General Motors and Jeep Compass declines, the share of exports going to the United States or any forecast.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a national production total and company examples, not demand or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a large share of Mexican vehicle output is exported, so a fall in production and exports points to lower North American assembly volumes, and plant closures and model transfers to the United States change where parts and materials are bought. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly is a large user of bonding, sealing and coating materials, and lower assembly in Mexico or a shift of models to US plants would redistribute that demand across suppliers' sites; the row gives no materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include the November production data, further plant closures or model transfers and US–Mexico trade policy.

El Financiero

item.title: OPEC+ pumped 41.23 million barrels a day in October, about 2.04 million more than in September, with Saudi Arabia up 26% to 10.563 million, its highest since February, The Globe and Mail and Lianhe Zaobao report.
item.description:
The Globe and Mail reports that the OPEC+ group, which includes OPEC and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million barrels a day in October, up around 2.04 million from September. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563 million barrels a day, up from 8.372 million in September and its highest since February, when it reported 10.882 million. Lianhe Zaobao puts the Saudi rise at 26% and says it shows that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf exporters have succeeded in restoring crude oil supplies despite the unresolved conflict and a series of Iranian attacks on tankers; it adds that Iraq reported a new war-time high of nearly 4.9 million barrels a day, well above its agreed production ceiling. Russia's output rose by 41,000 barrels a day to 8.668 million. The Economic Times says Strait of Hormuz traffic has averaged 10.5 million barrels a day since the start of October, according to Kpler, against 13.5 million before the war, and that total Gulf crude exports, counting routes that bypass Hormuz, have risen to an average of 16.7 million barrels a day against 17 million before the war. Saudi Arabia's rise (10.563 million against 8.372 million, a difference of about 2.19 million) is larger than the group's rise of around 2.04 million, and the rows do not say how the two figures are reconciled. They also do not give the group's production quotas, its pre-war output total, refined-product supply or how much of the extra crude has reached buyers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report crude production and export volumes, not prices or refined-product supply. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, crude oil and its derivatives are the feedstock and energy base of many resins, solvents and polymers, so a recovery in crude supply can ease availability, while shipping risk and the remaining gap to pre-war flows keep logistics costs and supply planning uncertain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, raw-material and energy costs reach the business through the petrochemical chain with a lag, so supply data of this kind show direction rather than price; the rows give no petrochemical or price figures. Points that may be worth considering include the November output figures, Hormuz transit volumes and the pace at which Gulf exports return to pre-war levels.

The Globe and Mail | Lianhe Zaobao | The Economic Times
